sections.title: Campaign Overview
sections.content: April 2026 was a month of steady ground-level intelligence gathering. The market showed clear signs of life — a meaningful number of prospects engaged in genuine conversation, and several meetings were secured — but the overall picture was one of a space that is increasingly crowded with incumbent solutions. A large proportion of the conversations reached were substantive enough to reveal real buying context, and the pipeline of callbacks and follow-ups built throughout the month suggests there is latent interest that has not yet converted. The month felt like planting seeds rather than harvesting, with the market broadly aware of the carbon reporting category but not yet compelled to move.
sections.content2: What stood out most was the prevalence of locked-in contracts and established internal processes. Prospects were rarely hostile to the concept of what Furthr offers — in fact, several expressed genuine curiosity — but they arrived at conversations already anchored to existing tools, consultants, or long-term agreements. This created a pattern where interest was present but timing was the blocker, rather than a fundamental rejection of the value proposition. The segment that proved hardest to crack was larger organisations with centralised sustainability functions, where decisions are made at head office level and frontline contacts have no mandate to evaluate new solutions.
sections.content3: On the positive side, the conversations that did open up revealed a market that is actively grappling with data complexity — particularly around scope three — and beginning to feel the limits of spreadsheet-based approaches and legacy integrations. Several prospects flagged that their current setups were functional but fragile, and at least one explicitly noted that data management was expected to become more challenging as volume increases. That is a window Furthr should be looking to open wider in the months ahead.

rows.what_said: A prospect confirmed they are currently engaged with PlanetMark for carbon accounting and not looking to expand until autumn, though they expressed future interest in breaking down emissions by fuel type.
Lisa stated that Mondra handles their sustainability data needs under a long-term contract, making Furthr's offer not currently relevant.
A sustainability manager noted their colleagues handle scope three reporting with third-party integration into SAP systems, indicating an embedded technical solution already in place.
Claire mentioned her team writes their own code for tracking carbon emissions and has previously evaluated external platforms, finding them too expensive and insufficiently flexible.
Emma noted they already have consultants and internal tools for carbon reporting and are not looking to bring in another third party.
A small charity representative mentioned using an associate for calculations and Excel, acknowledging this may become inadequate as data volume grows.
A sustainability manager cited their previous experience at Schneider Electric as having equipped them sufficiently for current scope three reporting demands.
A prospect stated their current solution is contractually locked in for three years, making any new offering irrelevant for now.

items.objection: Already using a solution or consultant
items.quote: They already have consultants and internal tools for their carbon reporting needs, so they aren't looking to hire another third party.
items.analysis: This was the dominant objection of the month, appearing across company sizes and sectors. It signals that the category is well understood but that Furthr is entering conversations after the buying decision has already been made. The focus should shift to uncovering contract end dates and positioning around the limitations of current solutions — particularly around flexibility, cost, and scalability — rather than leading with product features.

items.objection: Not the right person / handled elsewhere
items.quote: Sustainability reporting and carbon data management are handled by their head office, and he doesn't get involved in those matters.
items.analysis: A significant number of contacts, while reachable, had no decision-making authority over sustainability tools. This suggests the contact data may benefit from a review to better target sustainability leads at business-unit or group level. Where referrals were offered, they should be pursued immediately — and where they were not, switchboard escalation is a viable next step.

items.quote: They work with Mondra for their needs and it is a long-term contract, making my offer not relevant at this time.
items.analysis: Contract lock-in is a timing objection rather than a values objection. These prospects should be flagged for re-engagement six to nine months before their contract renewal window. The goal with these contacts is to plant doubt about their current solution's capabilities — particularly around scope three granularity and data volume — so that Furthr is front of mind when they next evaluate.

items.objection: Platform too expensive or not flexible enough
items.quote: Found them too expensive and lacking needed flexibility.
items.analysis: Price and configurability concerns indicate that prospects who have previously evaluated Furthr or similar platforms have unresolved questions about ROI and customisation. This objection warrants a dedicated response in outreach — either a clearer articulation of pricing tiers or proof points around platform flexibility, ideally backed by case studies from comparable organisations.

items.objection: Prefers not to receive cold calls / registered with TPS
items.quote: They don't take cold calls as they are registered with the telephone preference service.
items.analysis: A portion of the market is proactively opted out of cold outreach. This is a data quality and channel issue. Where TPS registrations are flagged, those contacts should be removed promptly and replaced with email or LinkedIn-first outreach to avoid compliance risk and to protect Furthr's brand reputation in the market.

items.objection: Not relevant to our sector or scale
items.quote: Their focus on social housing doesn't require much on carbon capture — they work with a consultant for that and don't have extensive reporting needs like the private sector.
items.analysis: Some prospects felt Furthr's proposition was calibrated for larger, more complex organisations. This is worth examining in terms of how the opening pitch is framed — particularly when calling into sectors like social housing, small charities, or niche B2B firms. A more sector-contextualised introduction could reduce early dismissal in these verticals.

items.question: How did you get my personal number?
items.analysis: Prospects are increasingly aware of data sourcing practices and are questioning the provenance of their contact details. This reveals a growing sensitivity around privacy in the sustainability space — likely professionals who are active on LinkedIn and receive high volumes of outreach. Transparency about data sourcing, offered proactively and confidently, can convert a defensive moment into a trust-building one.

items.question: Can you call back at a specific time?
items.analysis: The frequency of callback requests suggests genuine but time-pressured prospects rather than outright rejection. Many were mid-meeting or mid-task when reached. This is actually a positive signal — it indicates the contact was not hostile enough to decline outright. Rigorous callback scheduling and follow-through is critical to converting this latent interest into meetings.

items.question: Can you send an email instead?
items.analysis: Several prospects defaulted to email as their preferred channel, which often functions as a soft deflection but can also represent a genuine preference for asynchronous communication. A strong, concise follow-up email sequence — tailored to the specific context of each call — is essential to keep these prospects warm and move them toward a conversation.

items.heading: Scope three is the pressure point, not scope one or two
items.body: Multiple prospects referenced scope one and two reporting as essentially solved problems within their organisations, while scope three — with its supply chain complexity and third-party dependencies — was consistently flagged as the area of ongoing challenge. One prospect explicitly noted their colleagues handle scope three with third-party SAP integration, and another charity contact acknowledged that data management around scope three was expected to become more difficult as volume grows. Furthr's messaging should lean heavily into scope three as the primary pain point.

items.heading: The Excel-to-platform transition is still happening
items.body: A meaningful subset of organisations are still operating with spreadsheet-based approaches, often supplemented by an external associate or consultant. These contacts recognise the limitations but have not yet committed to a platform solution. The window for conversion is open but requires a clear articulation of what the transition looks like in practice — particularly around implementation burden and time-to-value.

items.heading: Centralised sustainability functions are blocking frontline access
items.body: In larger organisations, sustainability reporting is increasingly consolidated at group or head office level, leaving site-level or regional contacts unable to engage meaningfully with new solutions. This structural pattern means that cold outreach to individual sustainability managers at large enterprises is often a dead end unless it is paired with a strategy to access central procurement or group ESG leads directly.

items.heading: Prospects are fatigued by cold outreach in this category
items.body: Several contacts either hung up immediately, cited TPS registration, or expressed frustration at the volume of calls they receive. This suggests the sustainability reporting space is becoming increasingly saturated with vendor outreach, and that a differentiated opening — one that leads with insight or a specific sector reference rather than a generic product introduction — will be necessary to earn time in this market.

items.heading: Future interest is real but seasonally deferred
items.body: A recurring pattern across the month was prospects expressing genuine interest in the category but pointing to autumn or later in the year as their window for evaluation. One contact confirmed they were not looking to expand their current solution until autumn, and several others framed callbacks in terms of months rather than days. This suggests a pipeline-building phase now could yield a strong conversion period in Q3.

sections.title: Recommended Actions
items: Build a dedicated re-engagement sequence for contract-locked prospects — flag their estimated renewal windows and initiate outreach six to nine months prior, leading with a question about how their current solution handles scope three data volume and granularity.

Develop a sector-specific opening for social housing, small charities, and other lower-complexity verticals that acknowledges their scale and frames Furthr's value in terms of efficiency and audit-readiness rather than enterprise-level reporting complexity.

Prioritise immediate follow-up on all callback-committed contacts from April — the volume of deferred conversations represents the highest-probability pipeline, and each should receive a personalised confirmation email within 24 hours of the agreed callback time.

Review contact data quality to reduce the proportion of calls reaching non-decision-makers — focus on identifying group-level or head-office sustainability leads in larger organisations where frontline contacts consistently deflect to central teams.

Create a concise, insight-led follow-up email template for prospects who requested email communication — it should open with a scope three-specific insight or data point rather than a product pitch, to earn attention in an inbox likely to receive multiple vendor approaches.

Flag PlanetMark as a priority competitive focus — the prospect currently using PlanetMark expressed specific interest in breaking down emissions by fuel type, which represents a direct feature conversation Furthr should be prepared to have in depth as a differentiator during the scheduled Wednesday follow-up.

sections.title: Campaign Overview
sections.content: May was a month that revealed a market in genuine flux. A meaningful proportion of conversations surfaced prospects who are actively thinking about their next move — not just passively open to a conversation, but asking real questions and engaging with the proposition in detail. The activated and meetings-booked numbers reflect a cohort of decision-makers who recognised the problem Furthr solves and were willing to move quickly, which speaks well of how the proposition is landing when it reaches the right person.
sections.content2: That said, the shape of the 'no' responses tells its own story. The largest group of rejections came from people who said no definitively — not now, not ever — which on the surface sounds discouraging, but in practice suggests the targeting is reaching genuine decision-makers rather than gatekeepers or non-relevant contacts. People with no stake in the problem tend to deflect or redirect; people who say 'not ever' have usually already formed a view, which means the proposition is being understood. The referral rate from those who weren't the right person was modest, pointing to an opportunity to improve how those conversations are navigated to extract more value before they close.
sections.content3: The overall feel of the market in May was cautious but curious. There was a recurring sense that prospects are aware something needs to change in their current setup, but are weighing up timing, internal capacity, and perceived risk before committing. Conversations that broke through this hesitation tended to do so by anchoring quickly to a specific pain point rather than leading with a broad overview of what Furthr does. The pipeline generated this month has real potential, and the intelligence gathered sets a strong foundation for June.

rows.what_said: Prospects frequently described having a manual or ad hoc internal process they had built themselves, often acknowledging it was imperfect but familiar. Framed as 'we just do it ourselves for now' or 'we've always handled it internally.'

A recurring reference to 'the platform we already use' without naming it directly — often described as doing 'most of what we need' even if the prospect acknowledged gaps. Treated as the default they were reluctant to move away from.

Several prospects expressed genuine interest but cited an active procurement review or a board-level spend freeze as preventing any new vendor conversations from progressing. Not a rejection of Furthr specifically.

A small number of prospects indicated they had outsourced the relevant function to a consultant or external agency and did not feel empowered to evaluate alternatives without that party's involvement.

Mentioned almost affectionately — prospects were often self-aware that relying on spreadsheets was not sustainable but described switching away as a significant undertaking. One prospect noted 'it works until it doesn't.'

The most passive form of resistance — prospects who were not actively unhappy enough with the current situation to justify change. Often framed as 'it's not a priority right now' rather than a direct objection to Furthr.

items.quote: We're halfway through a project right now — come back to us in Q3 and it might be a different conversation.
items.analysis: This is the most common form of deferral and should not be read as disinterest. It typically signals a prospect who sees the relevance but cannot justify the distraction of a vendor evaluation during a busy period. The opportunity here is to agree a specific follow-up date immediately and treat this as a warm pipeline rather than a lost contact. A lightweight touchpoint — a relevant insight or case reference — in the intervening weeks can keep Furthr front of mind without applying pressure.

items.objection: We already have something in place
items.quote: We've got a system for that — it's not perfect but it does the job.
items.analysis: This objection masks a common reality: the existing solution is tolerated rather than valued. The phrase 'it does the job' rarely means 'it works brilliantly' — it tends to mean 'we've stopped noticing how much it costs us.' The most effective response is not to challenge the tool directly but to ask what 'doing the job' looks like in practice, which often surfaces the friction points the prospect has normalised. Furthr's positioning should focus on what the current setup cannot do rather than why it should be replaced wholesale.

items.quote: Honestly, budget is tight across the board — we're not taking on anything new until at least the autumn.
items.analysis: Budget objections in May are worth taking seriously given the broader economic climate, but they are rarely the whole story. In a number of cases this month, the budget objection emerged early — before the prospect had fully understood the proposition — which suggests it was being used as a reflexive deflection rather than a considered position. Where budget is a genuine constraint, the conversation is still valuable: understanding the timeline, the budget cycle, and the internal decision-making process means Furthr can re-enter at exactly the right moment.

items.objection: Need to involve others before deciding
items.quote: I'd need to loop in my director before we went any further — it's not just my call.
items.analysis: This is a healthy objection in the sense that it confirms the prospect is taking the conversation seriously enough to think about internal process. It also reveals that Furthr is often reaching a middle layer of management who have influence but not final authority. The recommended approach is to treat the initial contact as a champion-building conversation — equipping them with the right framing and materials to take the idea upward — rather than attempting to close before the right stakeholders are involved.

items.objection: Not sure it applies to us
items.quote: I'm not sure we're quite the right fit for what you're describing — we're a bit different to your typical customer.
items.analysis: This objection often reflects a gap in how the proposition has been contextualised rather than a genuine mismatch. Prospects who say this have usually heard a general description of Furthr and cannot yet see how it maps to their specific situation. The solution is a more sector-specific or role-specific opening that signals immediately that Furthr understands their world. When a prospect feels recognised early in the conversation, the 'not sure it applies' objection rarely surfaces.

items.objection: Too busy to engage right now
items.quote: This isn't a great time — can you send something over and I'll have a look when things calm down.
items.analysis: The request to 'send something over' is almost always a polite close to the conversation rather than a genuine commitment to review materials. The more productive response is to treat the busyness itself as a signal — ask what is consuming their time right now, and look for the connection between that pressure and what Furthr can address. If the timing genuinely cannot shift, a very specific call-back with a clear agenda is more likely to convert than a follow-up email into a busy inbox.

items.question: How does it actually work in practice?
items.analysis: This is the most encouraging question a prospect can ask — it signals they have cleared the initial scepticism hurdle and are now trying to visualise adoption. It tends to come from people who are genuinely evaluating rather than politely deflecting. The answer should be concrete, step-by-step, and ideally grounded in an example that mirrors their context. Abstract explanations at this stage risk losing momentum.

items.question: What does implementation look like and how long does it take?
items.analysis: Implementation anxiety is a reliable indicator that the prospect is seriously considering the proposition. They are not asking whether Furthr works — they are asking whether they can absorb the change. This is also a question that often conceals a concern about internal resource: who in their team would own this, and how much of their time would it demand? Clear, honest answers about the onboarding process — including realistic timelines and what Furthr takes off their plate — will significantly reduce this barrier.

items.question: Can you give me an example of a company like ours that uses it?
items.analysis: Social proof is being actively sought, which means prospects are not yet at the point of trusting the proposition on its own terms. This question comes most often from prospects who are intrigued but cautious — they want permission from a peer before they feel comfortable moving forward. Sector-specific case references or brief proof points that map closely to the prospect's profile will do more work than general testimonials.

items.question: How does pricing work?
items.analysis: Pricing questions at the cold call stage are a double-edged signal. On one hand, they confirm enough interest to begin mentally committing to a decision process. On the other, if the price is surfaced without sufficient context around value, it becomes a point of resistance rather than a motivator. The priority at this stage should be to defer a detailed pricing conversation to a discovery meeting, where the specific value for that prospect can be established first.

items.question: Who else in our sector uses this?
items.analysis: A slightly more specific version of the social proof question, and a signal that sector credibility matters to this cohort. Prospects asking this question are benchmarking Furthr against what they perceive to be the norms in their industry. Where Furthr has sector-relevant clients or use cases, naming them (where permitted) will accelerate trust. Where it does not, framing the transferability of the proposition clearly is essential.

items.question: What makes you different from what we currently use?
items.analysis: This is a comparison question being asked by prospects who already have a solution in place and are not immediately dissatisfied. It places Furthr in a position where differentiation needs to be earned rather than asserted. The most effective responses avoid direct criticism of the incumbent and instead focus on the specific capabilities or outcomes that Furthr delivers that the current solution does not — ideally anchored to something the prospect has already indicated matters to them.

items.heading: The status quo is comfortable enough — until it isn't
items.body: A dominant thread across May's conversations was the prevalence of prospects who are operating on legacy processes or makeshift solutions that are working just well enough to avoid a crisis. The trigger for change is rarely a proactive decision — it tends to be a moment of failure or a specific pressure point that makes the cost of inaction suddenly visible. Furthr's messaging will land better if it can name and anticipate those trigger moments rather than leading with capability.

items.heading: Timing pressure is real but often negotiable
items.body: Many of the timing-based deflections this month were genuine rather than evasive — prospects are navigating end-of-quarter pressures, internal projects, and leadership changes that make new vendor evaluations feel like an unwelcome addition. However, the same prospects were often willing to commit to a specific future conversation, suggesting the interest is latent rather than absent. Consistent, well-timed follow-up in June and July could convert a significant portion of this deferred pipeline.

items.heading: Middle management is engaging, but needs enabling
items.body: A recurring pattern this month was reaching contacts who were genuinely interested in Furthr but did not hold the authority to progress a decision unilaterally. Rather than treating this as a dead end, it represents an opportunity to build internal advocates who can carry the case upward. Equipping these contacts with a clear, concise summary of the value proposition — something they can share internally without misrepresenting it — would meaningfully improve conversion from conversation to meeting.

items.heading: Sector credibility is a threshold requirement
items.body: Prospects across multiple conversations flagged an implicit expectation that Furthr would understand their specific context before they were willing to engage seriously. Generic framing was met with polite scepticism; conversations that opened with a sector-specific reference point moved more quickly and with less resistance. This suggests that tailoring outreach by vertical — even at the level of the opening sentence — would have a measurable impact on conversion.

items.heading: The ROI conversation is not yet being triggered early enough
items.body: Very few prospects in May moved naturally to asking about outcomes or return on investment during the cold call conversation — instead, questions centred on how the product works and who else uses it. This suggests the value narrative is being received as an interesting product story rather than a business case. Shifting the framing earlier in the conversation to focus on what the problem is costing the prospect — in time, resource, or risk — would accelerate the conversations that are currently stalling at the interest stage.

sections.title: Recommended Actions
items: Build a structured follow-up sequence for the 'not right now' cohort — assign specific call-back dates agreed during the conversation, and create a lightweight touchpoint (a relevant insight, a brief case reference, or a single pointed question) to be sent between the initial call and the follow-up. This group represents the highest-conversion opportunity in the near-term pipeline.

Develop two or three sector-specific opening framings that signal immediately to the prospect that Furthr understands their world. The pattern this month is clear: conversations that opened with generic language met more resistance; those anchored in a recognisable context moved faster. Even a single tailored sentence at the start of the call can shift the dynamic.

Create a concise, shareable one-pager designed specifically for the 'I need to loop someone else in' scenario — not a brochure, but a focused document that frames the problem, the solution, and the relevant proof points in language a champion can use when presenting the idea internally without Furthr in the room.

Shift the pricing conversation protocol so that cost is consistently deferred to the discovery meeting, with a clear bridge: 'That's exactly what we'd want to cover properly in a conversation — pricing is structured around your specific situation, so a quick call would let us give you a number that actually means something.' This prevents pricing from becoming a cold-call objection before value has been established.

Review the targeting criteria for contacts to identify whether there is a pattern in the 'No, Not Me' outcomes — specifically whether these are reaching people too junior to be relevant or too senior to be the right first conversation. A refined entry-point hypothesis, even a small adjustment in seniority or function, could materially improve the referral rate and reduce the proportion of conversations that close without a forward step.

Invest in a small bank of sector-relevant proof points or outcome statements that can be deployed in response to the 'can you give me an example of a company like ours' question. These do not need to be full case studies — a single sentence naming a recognisable outcome in a recognisable context is often enough to clear the credibility barrier and keep the conversation alive.

spiced.situation: Wiebke Flach is the Sustainability Manager at Unison. She is responsible for carbon reporting across scope 1, 2, and 3 and is currently managing data collection manually — contacting suppliers individually to gather spend data. There is no mention of any existing technology platform in use; the process appears to be entirely manual and relationship-driven.
spiced.pain: Wiebke's immediate pain is not reporting — she explicitly stated she has no compliance requirements driving reporting right now. Her core problem is data collection. She needs to increase the quality and volume of data she collects from suppliers before reporting becomes viable. The current process of contacting suppliers one by one to request spend data is clearly manual, time-consuming, and unscalable. She confirmed this directly when Harry described the process: 'Exactly.'
spiced.impact: Because her data collection is insufficient, Wiebke cannot meaningfully increase her carbon reporting — her own words were 'I do need to increase our data collection before I can increase the reporting.' This creates a bottleneck where the entire reporting function is stalled upstream at the data gathering stage. The operational impact is that she is likely spending significant time on manual supplier outreach with inconsistent results, and the strategic impact is that she cannot progress her sustainability programme until this foundation is resolved.
spiced.critical_event: No specific deadline, regulatory trigger, or budget cycle was mentioned during the call. Wiebke confirmed there are currently no compliance requirements driving urgency around reporting. There is no confirmed critical event at this stage. The AE should probe for any internal targets, board-level sustainability commitments, or upcoming review cycles that might create a natural deadline.
spiced.decision: No information was gathered about the decision-making process, budget authority, stakeholders involved, or sign-off requirements. Wiebke agreed to the meeting readily, which suggests reasonable autonomy, but the AE should not assume she is the sole decision-maker. Nothing was established about budget availability or procurement process. This is a significant gap from the discovery call that the AE must address in the meeting.

objections.objection: Initial hesitation — Wiebke asked 'What company are you calling from?' in a tone suggesting unfamiliarity and mild suspicion about the call.
objections.response: Harry handled this smoothly by spelling out the company name and immediately pivoting to a relevant framing around sustainability managers and scope 1, 2, and 3 reporting. He did not dwell on it and moved quickly to qualification. This was handled well.

objections.objection: Wiebke clarified that reporting is not her priority and she has no compliance requirements: 'The reporting is — I have no compliance requirements in that regard. So yeah, it's all about the data collection, none about the reporting.'
objections.response: Harry acknowledged this and pivoted the conversation to data collection, which was the right instinct. However, he did not probe deeply into what specifically makes the data collection difficult, how many suppliers are involved, or what a better process would need to look like. The pivot was made but the discovery was left shallow. The AE should treat this as an open thread.

handovers.recommended_approach: Open the meeting by anchoring on Wiebke's own words: she cannot increase reporting until she improves data collection. Do not lead with the reporting or compliance angle — she was explicit that this is irrelevant to her right now. Frame the entire conversation around solving the upstream data collection problem. Early in the meeting, ask her to walk you through her current supplier data collection process in detail — how many suppliers she is contacting, how she tracks responses, what format the data comes back in, and where it breaks down. This will surface the real friction and allow you to map specific Furthr capabilities to specific steps in her workflow. You should also probe for what 'increasing data collection' means in measurable terms for her — is there a target number of suppliers, a coverage percentage, or an internal programme milestone she is working towards? This will help establish whether there is a critical event that did not emerge on the cold call. On the decision side, ask an open question about who else in the business would be involved in evaluating or implementing a new data collection process — procurement, IT, finance, or a sustainability director above her. Nothing was established on this and it is a priority gap to close. Finally, given the meeting scheduling was somewhat chaotic and a firm date did not appear to be locked in by the end of the call, confirm the meeting date and time directly with Wiebke before the AE joins.
key_quotes: It is relevant. I do need to increase our data collection before I can increase the reporting though.
The reporting is — I have no compliance requirements in that regard. So yeah, it's all about the data collection, none about the reporting.
Exactly. [Confirming she is currently contacting all suppliers manually to request spend data]
Yes. [Confirming she is currently working from spend data for her carbon calculations]

spiced.situation: James is the ESG Manager at Buzzacott, an accountancy and advisory firm. He is currently using a tool called Trace for embodied carbon and scope three reporting — they have used Trace both as a platform and on a consultancy basis. He describes himself as someone who supports the decision-making process around tools but is not the final decision-maker. Buzzacott is actively scoping what ESG tools are available, both for internal use and to potentially deliver services to clients in this space.
spiced.pain: Two distinct pain points emerged. First, internally, Buzzacott has an incomplete understanding of their own scope three emissions — specifically around procurement and purchased goods and services. James acknowledged they are not currently publishing scope three data, suggesting gaps in their ability to capture and interpret it. Second, from a commercial standpoint, Buzzacott wants to be able to offer ESG-related services to clients, but James explicitly said they are 'not quite in the place to actually be delivering services to clients right now' — meaning their current tooling or capability is insufficient to support client-facing delivery. The SDR also raised the broader market pain of data gathering being time-consuming and lacking actionable insights, which James did not push back on.
spiced.impact: The inability to fully understand scope three emissions has strategic and reputational consequences — James noted they need to 'bring it somewhat themselves to be able to sell it on,' meaning internal gaps are directly blocking a revenue opportunity. If Buzzacott cannot credibly demonstrate ESG capability, they cannot deliver those services to clients. On the internal side, even without a reporting obligation, James flagged that voluntary awareness of scope three — particularly around procurement — is important to him professionally and to the firm's positioning. The risk of falling behind on this is both commercial (losing client advisory revenue) and reputational (being seen as behind the curve on ESG).
spiced.critical_event: No hard deadline or regulatory trigger was explicitly mentioned. However, James described the scoping exercise as ongoing and active — they are currently assessing what tools are available. The combination of an existing tool (Trace) under review and a clear desire to move toward client-facing ESG services suggests there is momentum, but no specific date or event was cited that creates urgency. The AE should probe for whether there is an internal review cycle, a client pitch, or a reporting deadline driving the timeline.
spiced.decision: James is not the final decision-maker. He described his role as 'supporting in what is out there and what might be most appropriate for our purposes' and said he needs to discuss any information with 'my manager and some of the other parties.' He mentioned having 'a couple of people that I think could be interested.' No names, titles, or budget figures were shared. The process appears to be at an early scoping stage — James wants to gather information and present options upward. The AE should aim to understand who the manager is, what other parties are involved, and what the evaluation criteria look like.

objections.objection: We already use another tool called Trace — both the platform and on a consultancy basis.
objections.response: The SDR handled this adequately by asking a clarifying question about whether they use Trace as a consultancy or just the platform, which showed curiosity rather than panic. However, the SDR did not directly address what Furthr offers that Trace does not, nor did they probe for any dissatisfaction with Trace. The response about Furthr offering 'a suite of different software tools' and helping choose the right one was vague and did not land a clear differentiation. The AE must come prepared with a specific, honest comparison and lead with questions about where Trace is falling short before positioning Furthr.

objections.objection: I don't make the final call on these things.
objections.response: The SDR acknowledged this but did not probe further — no attempt was made to identify the decision-maker by name, understand the internal process, or ask what James would need to see in order to recommend Furthr internally. This is a significant gap. The AE should address this directly in the meeting and aim to either get the manager or other stakeholders involved in a subsequent call, or at minimum understand exactly what James needs to bring back to them.

handovers.recommended_approach: Open by referencing the two-track interest James mentioned — internal scope three visibility and the ambition to deliver ESG services to clients — and ask him which of those is the more pressing priority right now. This shows you have listened and lets him set the agenda. On the internal side, probe specifically into what Trace is and is not giving them around procurement and purchased goods and services — he was specific about that category, so go deeper there. Ask what their current process looks like for gathering that data and where it breaks down. On the client-facing side, ask what 'not quite in the place to deliver services' actually means — is it a capability gap, a credibility gap, a tooling gap, or all three? This is a commercial growth conversation as much as a compliance one, and that angle may resonate more strongly with James's manager when he takes this upward. Avoid leading with a product demo or feature walkthrough. James needs ammunition to present internally, so think about what a one-page summary or internal business case would look like for him. Before closing the meeting, make a direct ask to understand who else needs to be involved and whether it is possible to bring James's manager into the next conversation. Given that Trace is already embedded, do not dismiss it — ask what they like about it and where it leaves gaps. That is where Furthr's positioning should live.
key_quotes: We're sort of scoping out at the moment. So I would be interested certainly receiving some of your info that I can discuss with my manager and some of the other parties.

We're looking at our client position... not quite in the place to actually be delivering services to clients right now, but we're trying to understand what tools are out there that may be able to support with the delivery in that space.
